body_markdown:
Stellantis is investing $25 billion to bring 11 new models to the North American market in the coming years. The product offensive is part of a global, $70-billion investment[announced earlier in 2026](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/stellantis-7b-plan-means-11-new-vehicles-for-the-u-s-by-2030/) , and it will spawn numerous enthusiast-focused models from Jeep, Dodge, and Ram. Chrysler is also set to get new cars, according to a recent report, and Ram will launch its first SUV.


Stellantis[rebooted](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/srt-returns-at-stellantis-under-tim-kuniskis-leadership/) its Street and Racing Technology (SRT) division in 2025 to develop high-performance cars. Some will be amped-up versions of existing cars, while others will land as standalone models. Industry trade journal *[Automotive News](https://www.autonews.com/car-concepts/future-product/an-stellantis-future-product-0909/)* wrote that the list of SRT-developed cars in the pipeline includes a hot hatch named Dodge GLH and a muscle car called Dodge Copperhead.


Both will dust off a decades-old nameplate: The GLH (which stands for “Goes Like Hell”) was a sportier evolution of[the Omni](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/thanks-to-shelby-the-omni-glh-was-a-candle-in-a-dim-decade/) , while the Copperhead was released in 1997 as a concept that explored what a more affordable alternative to[the Viper](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/7-dodge-viper-facts-you-may-not-know-from-the-men-who-built-it/) could look like. Dodge doesn’t currently sell a hatchback, so it will be interesting to see what the next GLH is based on. Luckily, there are several European-market hatchbacks in the Stellantis portfolio. As for the Copperhead, it will slot near the top of the Dodge range.


Rumors of a V-8-powered version of[the new Dodge Charger](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/dodge-charger-550-horse-sixpack-no-hemi-no-problem/) have swirled around for years, but they’ve never materialized. Even[the 2027 Charger Super Bee](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/2027-dodge-charger-super-bee-pictures-specs-performance/) (shown below) uses a twin-turbo, 3.0-liter straight-six. It’s too early to tell if SRT will finally stuff[a Hemi V-8](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/oh-snap-the-hemi-v-8-returns-to-ram-pickup-lineup/) in the Charger, but one of the models it’s working on is a hotter evolution of the Charger fitted with a huge rear wing.

SRT will also develop high-horsepower SUVs for Jeep and Ram, according to *Automotive News* . Jeep is no stranger to track-ready models, but Ram has never released one; in fact, it’s never sold an SUV of any kind. The looming product offensive will change that: Ram’s future range includes its first SUV, a compact truck called Rampage, and a long-awaited mid-size truck named Dakota.


Moving away from the pavement, Jeep will begin delivering[the electric Recon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/first-look-2026-jeep-recon-offers-650-hp-and-doorless-off-roading/) in the coming weeks. The off-roader was designed when demand for electric cars was relatively high. The segment has shrunk since, so Jeep is expected to expand the range with a gasoline-burning version of the Recon in the coming years. It’s also working on a Wrangler-based halo model called Scrambler.


The report adds that Chrysler’s future is secure, at least for now. Three new crossovers due out in the coming years will end[its years-long product drought](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/will-chrysler-conjure-up-a-comeback/) . One is[the Airflow](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/chrysler-airflow-preview/) , which is a mid-size model with[a heritage-laced name](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/1934-chrysler-airflow-future-early/) . It was previewed in a video released earlier in 2026. The other two are called Arrow and Arrow Cross, respectively, and they’ll be badge-engineered variants of the Grizzly and Grizzly Fastback that Fiat recently introduced on the European market. They’ll both be smaller than the Airflow.


Don’t expect anything fancy from future Chrysler models: Affordability will be the brand’s main selling point. The odds of seeing a high-performance, V-8-powered version of a budget-friendly crossover are low, but Stellantis has done crazier things in the past.


Alfa Romeo will also expand its range with new crossovers, though details aren’t available yet, and we’re hoping that[the Giulia](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2024-alfa-romeo-giulia-competizione-review-a-plenty-sweet-pot-as-is/) gets replaced to take on[the next-generation BMW 3 Series](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/2027-bmw-3-series-m350-specs-performance/) . Fiat’s range will be limited to[the 500e](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/the-2024-fiat-500e-is-what-an-electric-car-should-be/) and[the Topolino](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/2026-fiat-topolino-ev-pricing-specs-launch-date/) , however.


The move toward high-octane performance is a major shift for Stellantis, which had planned to go EV-only[under previous leadership](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/carlos-tavares-stellantis-ceo-resigns/) .


The post[Stellantis Plans for a Big Performance Offensive and More Affordable Models](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/stellantis-new-model-pipeline-srt-jeep-dodge-ram/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
